# Results — Study 944 (How Much Leverage) on the real daily tape

*Generated by [`examples/verify.py`](../examples/verify.py). The instrument: a **constant
leverage multiple**, **reset daily**, on **SPY** daily **total-return** closes
(`yfinance`, `auto_adjust=True`). The borrowed sleeve `(L−1)` is financed at the
**^IRX** 13-week bill rate (act/360, previous close) **plus a 50 bps/yr spread
(PROXY)**; the notional the daily reset trades pays **1 bp one-way × NAV**. Excess
returns subtract the same bill rate, so every Sharpe below is excess-of-cash on both
sides. Window SPY∩^IRX **2003-06-04 → 2026-06-30**. As-of **2026-06-30** (the partial
current month is dropped).*

## Data stamp

| Legs | Window | n days | Fingerprint |
|---|---|---|---|
| SPY (total return), ^IRX (bill rate) | 2003-06-04 → 2026-06-30 | 5,799 | Fingerprint `d6dfd514b42d` |

```
[data] SPY x ^IRX: 5,801 rows  2003-06-02 -> 2026-06-30  as-of 2026-06-30  fingerprint=be204d0845b7
```

(The [`quantlab.repro`](../../../quantlab/repro.py) stamp counts the two raw close series;
the 5,799 figure is the return frame, two rows shorter after the first difference and the
^IRX alignment.)

**Financing cross-check.** Over 2007-05-31 → 2026-06-30 the ^IRX-implied cash accrual
returns **1.47%/yr** against **BIL**'s realised total return of **1.36%/yr** — a gap of
**+11 bps/yr**, an order of magnitude inside the 0–200 bps spread sweep below. ^IRX is
used rather than BIL because it covers the whole window; BIL only starts in 2007.

**Window caveat — and it is not decorative.** The sample is gated by the cached ^IRX
history and starts in **2003-06**: it contains the GFC and 2022, but **not** the 2000–2002
bust. Section (4) below measures exactly how much that arbitrary left edge is worth, and
the answer is: *most of the study's headline*. Survivorship sits on the *Signal* axis here
in its macro form — this is one realisation of one index that did not suffer a terminal
decade, and the whole result is conditional on it.

## The leverage curve (daily reset, financed, costed)

| L | terminal | CAGR | g(L) | excess Sharpe | vol | max drawdown | turnover/yr |
|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| 1.00 | 11.68× | +11.27% | +10.68% | +0.575 | 18.6% | −55.2% | 0.0× |
| 1.50 | 22.81× | +14.56% | +13.59% | +0.566 | 27.8% | −72.6% | 1.4× |
| 2.00 | 36.35× | +16.90% | +15.61% | +0.560 | 37.1% | −84.2% | 3.8× |
| 2.50 | 47.17× | +18.23% | +16.75% | +0.557 | 46.4% | −91.3% | 7.2× |
| **2.85** | **49.99×** | **+18.53%** | **+17.00%** | +0.555 | 52.9% | **−94.5%** | 10.1× |
| 3.00 | 49.66× | +18.49% | +16.97% | +0.555 | 55.7% | −95.5% | 11.5× |

- **Realised growth-optimal multiple: 2.85.** Theoretical Kelly `mu/sigma²` on the same
  tape is **3.10**; the financing spread and the fat left tail pull the realised peak
  below the Gaussian formula, exactly as theory says they must.
- **Sharpe is invariant by construction.** At 0 bps spread and 0 cost the excess Sharpe
  is **0.5752 at L = 1 and 0.5752 at L = 3** — identical to four decimals. Constant
  leverage is a pure scaling of the excess return stream; it can only *lower* Sharpe,
  through the spread (0.575 → 0.555 at the optimum). **There is no risk-adjusted gain
  anywhere on this curve.** Everything the sweep can say is about *growth*, and growth is
  bought with drawdown: the realised optimum runs a **−94.5%** peak-to-trough.

## Is the optimum knowable? (1) block bootstrap of the argmax

Circular block bootstrap, 1,000 draws, 63-day (quarterly) blocks of the joint
`(r_asset, r_cash, acc)` rows, re-running the whole grid on each resample:

| point | 95% CI | sd | draws at the 1.0 floor | draws at the 3.0 cap |
|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| 2.85 | **[1.00, 3.00]** | 0.60 | 2.9% | 44.4% |

**The CI is the entire grid.** After 23 years of daily data the location of the peak is
not identified at all. This is not a defect of the estimator — it is the arithmetic of
the problem: `L* = mu/sigma²`, and `mu` is the slowest-converging quantity in finance.

## Is the optimum knowable? (2) rolling five-year ex-post optimum

217 monthly-stride windows of 1,260 days, each solved with **perfect hindsight inside the
window** — the easiest version of the question:

| windows | mean | sd | range | at floor 1.0 | at cap 3.0 |
|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| 217 | 2.36 | 0.86 | **[1.00, 3.00]** | 24.0% | 54.4% |

The rolling Kelly estimate itself ranges **−1.53 to +10.82**. Year-end readings: 1.00
through 2008–2012 (the GFC window), then 3.00 from 2013 onward apart from 2.05 in 2022,
2.85 in 2023 and 2.80 in 2024. The hindsight answer is "don't lever at all" for five
consecutive years and "lever as hard as the grid allows" for most of the following
thirteen.

## Is the optimum knowable? (3) era cut, and the era hand-off

| Era | n | realised optimum | Kelly | CAGR @opt | CAGR @L=1 | DD @L=1 | DD @L=3 |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| 2003-06-04 → 2014-12-31 | 2,911 | **2.20** | 2.37 | +11.93% | +8.82% | −55.2% | −95.5% |
| 2015-01-02 → 2026-06-30 | 2,888 | **3.00** (capped) | 3.99 | +27.07% | +13.80% | −33.7% | −76.2% |

The two decades do not agree on the answer: 2.20 against a *capped* 3.00, with the
underlying Kelly estimate nearly doubling (2.37 → 3.99). Transplanting one era's answer
into the other costs real growth in both directions:

- the **late** optimum (3.00) applied in the **early** era earns **+10.56%/yr** against
  **+8.82%** unlevered — it stays ahead, but it buys that 1.7 pp with a **−95.5%**
  drawdown, i.e. an account that no longer exists;
- the **early** optimum (2.20) applied in the **late** era earns **+23.52%** against
  **+27.07%** at the late optimum — a 3.6 pp/yr shortfall for using the wrong decade's
  number.

*(An earlier draft of this study ran on a cache whose ^IRX began 2004-01-06 and reported
the hand-off as a **loss** to not levering at all: +7.07% vs +7.81%. That sign flip, caused
by nothing but seven extra months at the front of the sample, is what motivated the
section below. It is reported rather than quietly overwritten.)*

## Is the optimum knowable? (4) start-date sensitivity — the sharpest number here

The same code, the same as-of date, the same instrument; only the **left edge of the
window** moves. The split date for the hand-off is held fixed at 2015-01-01 so the eras
stay comparable:

| sample start | n | realised optimum | Kelly | CAGR @opt | CAGR @L=1 | hand-off: late opt in early era | vs unlevered | **edge** |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| 2003-06-04 | 5,799 | 2.85 | 3.10 | +18.53% | +11.27% | +10.56% | +8.82% | **+1.73%/yr** |
| 2004-01-06 | 5,651 | 2.75 | 2.94 | +17.03% | +10.83% | +7.07% | +7.81% | **−0.74%/yr** |
| 2005-01-03 | 5,401 | 2.65 | 2.88 | +16.86% | +10.88% | +5.67% | +7.63% | **−1.96%/yr** |
| 2007-01-03 | 4,901 | 2.60 | 2.79 | +16.80% | +10.95% | +2.66% | +6.98% | **−4.32%/yr** |
| 2010-01-04 | 4,145 | 3.00 | 4.55 | +31.00% | +14.28% | +40.49% | +15.38% | **+25.11%/yr** |

Read the last column. Depending on where an analyst starts the sample — a choice with no
economic content whatsoever — the study's central qualitative claim reads either "one
decade's optimal leverage still beat not levering in the other" (+1.73%/yr) or "it lost
to doing nothing" (−4.32%/yr). **Seven months** of extra history at the front is enough to
flip the sign. The 2010 row is the same lesson at full volume: start after the GFC and the
"realised optimum" pins to the grid cap with a Kelly estimate of 4.55 — the tape says
lever 4.5× because the only crash in the sample has been deleted.

This is the study's finding, stated as strongly as the data permits: the *shape* of the
growth curve is stable, and the *location of its peak is a function of the sample you
happen to hold*.

## The tradable version — ex-ante Kelly (trailing 756 days, acted at t+1)

The study's **single execution lag**: `mu/sigma²` is estimated on the trailing three years
of daily excess returns through day *t*, clipped to [1.0, 3.0], and applied at *t+1*.
Window 2006-06-08 → 2026-06-30 (n = 5,043). The applied multiple averages **2.53** and
sits **at the 3.0 cap on 64.0% of days**, at the 1.0 floor on 16.8%.

| Arm | terminal | CAGR | excess Sharpe | vol | max drawdown |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| ex-ante Kelly | 33.95× | +19.26% | +0.597 | 41.2% | −71.6% |
| fixed L = 1.00 | 8.61× | +11.36% | +0.567 | 19.4% | −55.2% |
| fixed L = 2.00 | 22.35× | +16.79% | +0.553 | 38.9% | −84.2% |
| fixed L = 2.85 | 27.16× | +17.94% | +0.548 | 55.4% | −94.5% |
| fixed L = 3.00 | 26.47× | +17.79% | +0.547 | 58.3% | −95.5% |

- **vs L = 1:** log-growth advantage **+6.86%/yr**, HAC *t* = **+1.20**, block-bootstrap
  95% CI **[−5.56%, +17.52%]** — comfortably includes zero. (The arithmetic-excess *t* is
  **+2.54**, and it would clear the bar — but that statistic is mechanically inflated by
  the higher-volatility arm and is **not** the terminal-wealth test. Growth is additive in
  logs, so the log-difference is the statistic a compounding claim must clear. Both are
  printed so the divergence is visible rather than exploited.)
- **vs L = 2:** advantage +2.09%/yr, HAC *t* = **+0.56**. Against a fixed multiple picked
  out of a hat, the "optimal" rule adds nothing measurable.
- **The one place Sharpe can move.** Constant leverage cannot touch Sharpe, but this arm
  is *time-varying*, so it can — and it does, by **+0.030** (0.597 vs 0.567). Paired
  block bootstrap: 95% CI **[−0.180, +0.254]**, 59% of draws positive. Not distinguishable
  from zero, and roughly a tenth the size of the noise band.
- **The advantage is a function of the cap, not the signal.** Cap 1.5 → +2.78%/yr
  (*t* = +1.74); cap 2.0 → +4.63% (*t* = +1.46); cap 2.5 → +5.91% (*t* = +1.30); cap 3.0 →
  +6.86% (*t* = +1.20). More cap, more return, *less* significance — the classic signature
  of a scaling knob rather than an edge. The estimation window behaves the same way
  (252d → +3.46%/yr *t* = +0.71; 504d → +4.95% *t* = +0.93; 1,260d → +5.12% *t* = +0.78).
  **No configuration clears |*t*| = 2; the best anywhere in the design space is +1.74.**

## PROXY sweeps — the two non-tape assumptions

Neither the financing spread nor the reset cost is measured; both are labelled
assumptions and both are swept.

| Financing spread (bps/yr) | optimum | CAGR @opt | excess Sharpe @opt (vs +0.575 unlevered) | DD @opt |
|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| 0 | 3.00 | +19.71% | +0.573 | −95.4% |
| 25 | 2.95 | +19.11% | +0.564 | −95.1% |
| 50 (headline) | 2.85 | +18.53% | +0.555 | −94.5% |
| 100 | 2.75 | +17.45% | +0.539 | −93.8% |
| 200 | 2.45 | +15.56% | +0.509 | −91.0% |

| Reset cost (bps one-way) | optimum | CAGR @opt | turnover/yr |
|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| 0 | 2.90 | +18.66% | 10.5× |
| 1 (headline) | 2.85 | +18.53% | 10.1× |
| 5 | 2.80 | +18.06% | 9.6× |

The optimum moves smoothly with the spread and barely at all with the reset cost — the
daily reset is cheap; the *borrow* is what bites. At every assumption the excess Sharpe at
the optimum is **below** the unlevered Sharpe. Note that the whole 0–200 bps spread sweep
moves the optimum by 0.55 — *less* than the 0.40-plus that the arbitrary start date moves
it, and far less than the bootstrap's grid-wide CI.

## Synthetic control (machinery proof only — never supports the stamp)

An i.i.d. Student-*t* tape with a **planted** growth-optimal leverage of 2.0, and a null
version with zero excess drift, 40 years each, 8 seeds:

| tape | realised optimum (mean of 8 seeds) | per-seed spread | Kelly estimate (mean) |
|---|--:|---|--:|
| planted Kelly = 2.0 | **1.91** | 1.0, 1.0, 1.0, 1.5, 2.25, 2.5, 3.0, 3.0 | 2.04 |
| null (zero excess drift) | **0.44** | 0.0 × 4, 0.25, 0.5, 1.0, 1.75 | 0.01 |

The harness recovers the planted optimum on average and stays on the floor under the null
— it is unbiased. Conditionally it is near-exact: on the seed-944 tape the realised argmax
is **3.05** against that tape's own in-sample Kelly of **3.04**.

**The per-seed spread is the finding, restated.** Even in a *stationary, i.i.d., known*
world, forty years of daily data locates the growth-optimal multiple only to about ±1.
The real tape is worse, not better: it is non-stationary as well as noisy.

## Verdict

- **Signal — Weak.** Levering the index above 1× did raise realised growth on this tape,
  in both eras and at every assumption — the curve is real and its peak (2.85) sits
  sensibly below the Kelly formula (3.10). But the *claim* under test is that the optimum
  is a locatable number, and it is not: the bootstrap CI for the argmax is the **whole
  grid [1.00, 3.00]**, the five-year hindsight optimum spends 24% of windows at the floor
  and 54% at the cap, the realised optimum wanders 2.60 → 3.00 (and the Kelly estimate
  2.79 → 4.55) on the *start date alone*, and the tradable ex-ante Kelly rule's growth
  advantage over plain buy-and-hold is **+6.86%/yr with HAC *t* = +1.20** and a CI
  spanning zero — with **no** cap or estimation window reaching |*t*| = 2 (best: +1.74).
  Positive sign everywhere, significance nowhere.
- **Tradability — Mirage.** There is nothing risk-adjusted to bank: the excess Sharpe is
  **invariant in L by construction** (0.5752 at 1× and at 3× gross of the spread) and only
  ever falls once financing is paid (0.555 at the optimum). The one arm that *can* move
  Sharpe — the time-varying ex-ante rule — moves it by +0.030 with a 95% CI of
  [−0.180, +0.254]. The growth gain is purchased with a **−94.5%** drawdown at the
  realised optimum and −95.5% at 3× — losses that end a levered account long before the
  compounding argument gets to play out. And the number you would have to know is
  unknowable: it is not merely noisy, it is a function of where you start looking
  (+1.73%/yr or −4.32%/yr for the identical hand-off test, depending on the sample's left
  edge). "Optimal leverage" is a quantity that exists in hindsight and dissolves on
  contact with a forecast.
- **What is honestly true.** The shape of the curve — concave, peaking somewhere between
  1× and 3×, with Sharpe flat and drawdown catastrophic on the right-hand side — is
  robust. The *location* of the peak is not, and the location is the entire practical
  question.
